title: Trade war flare-up will cost Canada
gist: New US Section 338 tariffs of 50% on a slice of Canadian exports, plus threatened Canadian retaliation, are forecast to cut Canada's 2027 GDP by 0.3ppts and lift consumer prices by about 0.3ppts, with Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario manufacturers hit hardest.

insights.claim: The US-Canada trade war escalated after bilateral trade negotiations collapsed the week before August 28, 2026, with the US imposing 50% tariffs under Section 338 on about 5.5% of Canada's 2025 exports to the US, applied regardless of USMCA compliance.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: USMCA compliance no longer shields exporters from tariff risk, signaling the trade dispute has moved past the trade agreement's normal guardrails.
insights.quote: The US has imposed 50% tariffs through Section 338 on around 5.5% of Canada’s 2025 exports to the US. The tariffs apply regardless of USMCA compliance.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics estimates the new Section 338 tariffs will raise the overall US effective tariff rate on Canadian exports to 6.9% from 5.1%, with plastics, electrical machinery, and wood and paper products contributing the most to the increase.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Names the specific export sectors (plastics, electrical machinery, wood and paper) facing the sharpest tariff cost increase, useful for identifying exposed Canadian producers.
insights.quote: we estimate that the new tariffs will raise the US effective tariff rate on Canadian exports to 6.9% from 5.1%, with tariffs on plastics, electrical machinery, and wood and paper products contributing the most to the increase.

insights.claim: Canada has threatened dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs against the new US levies effective September 8, 2026, but as of the report's writing had not released details of which products would be affected.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The retaliation is announced but unspecified, so downstream sector impact and Oxford Economics' provincial modeling remain provisional until product-level detail emerges.
insights.quote: Canada has threatened to impose dollar-for-dollar tariffs in retaliation to the new US levies on September 8, though details of affected products haven’t been released.

insights.claim: If Canada's retaliation is proportional, applying 50% tariffs on roughly C$28 billion of Canadian imports from the US, Oxford Economics estimates it would raise Canada's effective tariff rate on the US by about 3.9 percentage points to just over 6%.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of Canada's likely counter-tariff exposure (C$28bn), giving a concrete base for estimating knock-on costs to US exporters into Canada.
insights.quote: We estimate that proportional retaliation, with 50% tariffs on roughly C$28bn of Canadian imports from the US, would raise Canada’s effective tariff rate on the US by about 3.9ppts to just over 6%.

insights.claim: Using its Global Economic Model, Oxford Economics forecasts that the combination of US Section 338 tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs will reduce Canada's GDP by 0.3 percentage points below its August 2026 baseline forecast in 2027, and lift Canadian consumer prices by around 0.3 percentage points in the following year.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Puts a concrete magnitude on the trade war's macro cost to Canada, a data point investors can weight against Bank of Canada policy expectations and Canadian growth forecasts.
insights.quote: we estimate that the combination of the Section 338 US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs will reduce Canada’s GDP by 0.3ppts below our August baseline forecast in 2027 and lift consumer prices by around 0.3ppts next year.

insights.claim: The targeted, sector-specific nature of the 50% US Section 338 tariffs means manufacturers based in Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario will be hit hardest among Canadian provinces.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Identifies specific provincial manufacturing bases (Quebec, New Brunswick, Ontario) as the geographic concentration of tariff risk, relevant for regional economic and political exposure.
insights.quote: The targeted nature of 50% US Section 338 tariffs means manufacturers in Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario will be affected the most.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics plans to update its provincial-level impact analysis using its bottom-up Canada Provincial Territorial Model once the details of Canada's retaliatory tariffs are released.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Signals that current provincial impact estimates are preliminary and a more granular, model-based update is forthcoming once retaliation specifics are public.
insights.quote: We’ll update this analysis using our bottom-up Canada Provincial Territorial Model once the details of the retaliatory tariffs are released.
